---
title: "Get started with dazdiff"
description: "Compare a table against a benchmark, read the result, and use the comparison in tests."
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 120)
```

```{r setup}
library(dazdiff)
```

We take one table through a round trip that changed it, compare it with the
original, and find out what changed and where. By the end you can run a
comparison, read its result, set a tolerance, compare two tables as equals,
and turn the comparison into a test. Every argument is described in
`?diff_table`.

## Compare against a benchmark

The benchmark is a small sales table. `stored` is the same data after a round
trip through storage. On the way, the column names changed case, the ids
became text, `units` came back as a double, a load timestamp was added, one
row was lost and one was added:

```{r}
benchmark <- data.frame(
  id     = c(1L, 2L, 3L, 4L),
  region = c("north", "south", "east", "west"),
  amount = c(100, 200, 300, 400),
  units  = c(10L, 20L, 30L, 40L)
)
stored <- data.frame(
  ID        = c("1", "2", "3", "5"),
  Region    = c("north", "south", "east", "north"),
  Amount    = c(100, 200.5, 300, 500),
  Units     = c(10.4, 20, 30, 50),
  loaded_at = "2026-09-29"
)
```

`diff_table()` takes the benchmark first. Rows are paired on their
**identity**, the `by` columns, and the **measures** are the numeric columns
compared value by value. Measures default to `"numeric"`, the double
columns; `"numeric+integer"` adds the integer `units`:

```{r}
d <- diff_table(benchmark, stored, by = c("id", "region"), measures = "numeric+integer")
d
```

The messages say what the comparison did on the way. `loaded_at` is not in the
benchmark, so it was dropped. `stored`'s columns were cast to the benchmark's
types, and `Units`' `10.4` became the integer `10`. That cast is recorded,
with the rows it touched, in `attr(d, "truncated")`; `truncate = FALSE`
refuses it instead.

The result is a `data.table`, with one row per compared value:

- **`status`** is `same`, `changed`, `only_x` (the row is missing from the
  tested table) or `only_y` (the row exists only there).
- **`row_id_x` and `row_id_y`** are the row numbers in the two inputs, so
  every difference traces back to its source.
- **`diff`** is `value_y - value_x`, **`abs_diff`** its size, and
  **`rel_diff`** the size relative to the larger of the two values.

Column names are **normalized** in both tables, to upper case with other
characters turned into `_`. That is why `id` and `ID` pair up.

## Summarize the comparison

`diff_summary()` condenses the result to one row per measure, with the counts
of each status and the size of the differences:

```{r}
diff_summary(d)
```

`diff_report()` draws the whole comparison as text: the columns compared, how
the rows of the two tables align, and how much each measure differs. Name the
two tables for the drawing:

```{r}
diff_report(d, x_name = "benchmark", y_name = "stored")
```

## Allow a tolerance

`diff_table()` is exact by default. A value is `same` when it is within
`tolerance` (absolute) or `rel_tol` (relative to the larger magnitude). With
`rel_tol = 0.01`, the half unit on 200 passes, and only the rows missing from
one table remain:

```{r}
d_tol <- diff_table(benchmark, stored, by = c("id", "region"),
                    measures = "numeric+integer", rel_tol = 0.01)
d_tol[status != "same"]
```

To ask one comparison at several thresholds without running it again, use
`is_matching()`. It is `TRUE` only when every value is `same`, so the rows
found in one table keep it `FALSE` at any threshold. Among the rows found in
both, the threshold decides:

```{r}
is_matching(d, rel_tol = 0.01)
both <- d[status %in% c("same", "changed")]
is_matching(both)
is_matching(both, rel_tol = 0.01)
```

## Find where the differences are

`diff_explain()` says which key columns split the rows that match from the
ones that do not. A column **separates** them when none of its values is
`mixed`: knowing the value tells whether the record matches. A column with a
different value on every row, like `ID`, always separates and so explains
nothing; it is marked **identifies** and listed last. Here no other column
separates:

```{r}
diff_explain(d)
```

Given a column, it lists that column's values, with each classed as `same`,
`differ` or `mixed`:

```{r}
diff_explain(d, "region")
```

## Compare two tables as equals

The default `mode = "benchmark"` takes the first table's types as the truth.
`mode = "equal"` compares the two tables as peers: nothing is cast or
dropped, and every column must be in both with the same type. So `stored`
does not compare with the benchmark at all:

```{r, error = TRUE}
diff_table(benchmark, stored, mode = "equal")
```

Row order never matters, because rows are aligned on their identity. With no
`by`, the identity is every column that is not a measure:

```{r}
diff_table(benchmark, benchmark[c(4, 1, 2, 3), ], mode = "equal")
```

In either mode, a comparison with no measures compares rows as wholes,
which answers "do the two tables have the same rows?". A repeated row counts once per copy, numbered by
`key_seq`:

```{r}
diff_table(
  benchmark[c("id", "region")],
  data.frame(ID = c(3L, 1L, 2L, 2L), REGION = c("east", "north", "south", "south"))
)
```

A key that repeats in a comparison with measures is paired in arrival order,
with a warning. `duplicates = "aggregate"` compares the repeats as multisets
instead, and `duplicates = "error"` refuses them. A table with no key column
at all can get a virtual one: `row_key = "position"` pairs rows as they come,
and `row_key = "sorted"` pairs them after sorting both tables by their
values.

## Use it in tests

`expect_table_equal()` is a testthat expectation built on `diff_table()`. Its
second argument, `expected`, is the benchmark, as in testthat's
`expect_equal()`. Like any expectation, it is silent when it passes, here on
the same rows in another order:

```{r}
reference <- benchmark
expect_table_equal(benchmark[c(4, 1, 2, 3), ], reference)
```

Unlike `diff_table()`, it allows a relative difference of
`sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)` (about `1.5e-8`) by default, as `expect_equal()`
does, so floating-point noise does not fail a test. Pass `rel_tol = 0` to
compare exactly. A failure shows `diff_summary()` and the first records that
differ. A key that repeats is an error rather than a guess, unless you pass
`duplicates = "disambiguate"` or `duplicates = "aggregate"`.

In a test file it reads like any other expectation:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
test_that("the pipeline reproduces the reference output", {
  expect_table_equal(run_pipeline(), reference)
})
```
